title: Deeds and grace
hook: deeds shape the body we are given; grace opens the door

segments.voice: Yesterday, order and effort: everyone within the hukam, and still the Gurus ask us to strive. Your line: strive within the order.

Two words side by side in the fourth pauri of Japji: karmi, nadri. In paraphrase, the line runs: by deeds comes the robe; by grace, the door of liberation. A robe and a door. An odd pair for one breath. A robe is something you're wrapped in every day; it takes the shape of you. A door is something you can stand in front of for a very long time and never open with your own hand. Today's word is the first half: karam.
screen: `A ROBE AND A DOOR.` → `KARMI, NADRI.` → `TODAY'S WORD: THE FIRST HALF.`

segments.voice: The robe first. Sikh readers take the robe in this line as the body, the life we're given. Karam is deeds, actions and their weight. What we have done shapes what we carry: the body, the circumstances, the habits that wrap around us. On its own, that would be a strict ledger. Then the door. Nadar is the glance, the gracious look of the One. The line says the door of liberation opens by nadar, not by karam. You can do good for a lifetime, and the door still isn't something you buy. It is given. Why both? If the line said only deeds, life would be bookkeeping, and anyone behind would stay behind. If it said only grace, there'd be no reason to do good at all. Guru Nanak keeps both: deeds really do shape us, and the last step is a gift. The same pauri closes, in paraphrase: the True One is all of it. Readers hold the line in two ways. Some Sikh interpreters read karmi itself as grace, so the robe, too, would be a gift. Others read it as deeds, as today does. Both readings keep grace at the door. So the life this points to looks like yesterday's farmer: do the good in front of you with your whole heart, and leave the door to the giver. Deeds and grace.
screen: `KARAM: DEEDS SHAPE THE ROBE.` · `NADAR: GRACE OPENS THE DOOR.` · `NOT A LEDGER, NOT AN EXCUSE.` · `DO THE GOOD; LEAVE THE DOOR.` · then, large: `DEEDS AND GRACE.`

segments.voice: Picture one good deed within reach today, carrying something for someone, a kind word to a coworker, a bill paid fairly, and see yourself doing it. Let the picture end the moment the deed is done, and let the result belong to someone else. If you pray, let that letting go become a hope for grace; if you don't, just feel the difference between doing and receiving.
Karam. Deeds, actions and their weight: in Japji, by deeds comes the robe, and by grace, nadar, the door of liberation. Today's word.
Your line: deeds and grace. The robe is worn; the door is given. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning, including the line about deeds and the robe, grace and the door, and Sikh life joins seva and honest work with remembrance and trust in the Guru's grace.
